import FormalConjecturesUtil
/-!
# Equidistributed Sequences

Corollary 4.2 of Chapter 1 states that the sequence $(x^n), n = 1, 2, ... ,$ is equidistributed modulo 1 for
almost all x > 1. And a little bit further down:
"one does not know whether sequences such as $(e^n)$, $(π^n)$, or even $((\frac 3 2)^n)$"
are equidistributed modulo 1 or not.

*References:*
  - [Uniform Distribution of Sequences](https://store.doverpublications.com/products/9780486149998)
by *L. Kuipers* and *H. Niederreiter*, 1974
  - [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Equidistributed_sequence)
-/

namespace Equidistribution

open scoped Topology

/--
A point `x` is an accumulation point of a sequence `s_0, s_1, ...`
if any neighbourhood of `x` contains a point of the sequence distinct
from `x`.
-/
def IsAccumulationPoint (x : ℝ) (s : ℕ → ℝ) : Prop :=
  x ∈ closure (Set.range s \ {x})

/--
If a point `x` is an accumulation point of a sequence `s_0, s_1, ...` then
there is a subsequence of `s` that tends to `x`
-/
@[category textbook, AMS 11 54]
theorem isAccumulationPoint_exists_subsequence_tendsto
    (x : ℝ) (s : ℕ → ℝ) (hx : IsAccumulationPoint x s) :
    ∃ (u : ℕ → ℕ), StrictMono u ∧ Filter.atTop.Tendsto (s ∘ u) (𝓝 x) := by
  sorry

/--
The sequence `(3/2)^n` is equidistributed modulo `1`.
-/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem isEquidistributedModuloOne_three_halves_pow :
    IsEquidistributedModuloOne (fun n => (3 / 2 : ℝ)^n) := by
  sorry

/-- For any transcendental number `x`, the sequence `x * (3 / 2) ^ n` is
equidistributed modulo 1. -/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem isEquidistributedModuloOne_transcendental_three_halves_pow (x : ℝ)
    (hx : Transcendental ℚ x) :
    IsEquidistributedModuloOne (fun n ↦ x * (3 / 2 : ℝ) ^ n) := by
  sorry

/--
The sequence `(3/2)^n` has infinitely many accumulation points modulo `1`.
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 11]
theorem isAccumulationPoint_three_halves_pow_infinite :
    {x | IsAccumulationPoint x (fun n => Int.fract <| (3 / 2 : ℝ)^n)}.Infinite := by
  sorry

/--
Find an accumulation point of the sequence `(3/2)^n` modulo `1`.
-/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem isAccumulationPoint_three_halves_pow :
    IsAccumulationPoint answer(sorry) (fun n => Int.fract <| (3 / 2 : ℝ)^n) := by
  sorry

/--
There is an accumulation point of the sequence `(3/2)^n` modulo `1`.
-/
@[category test, AMS 11]
theorem isAccumulationPoint_three_halves_pow_exists :
    ∃ p, (IsAccumulationPoint p (fun n => Int.fract <| (3 / 2 : ℝ)^n)) := by
  sorry

end Equidistribution

findings.description: Lines 65–67 assert equidistribution for every transcendental real multiplier x. The cited book gives an almost-everywhere statement, not a statement excluding only algebraic exceptions. These are genuinely different: Flatto–Lagarias–Pollington report that the set of positive ξ satisfying 4/65 ≤ {ξ(3/2)^n} < 61/65 for every n ≥ 0 is uncountable. Since algebraic reals are countable, this set contains transcendental multipliers. For each such multiplier, the frequency in [0,2/65] is identically zero instead of tending to 2/65, contradicting the Lean conclusion. Thus this is a false strengthening of the source, not merely a faithfully stated conjecture with an outdated status.
findings.source_evidence: Kuipers–Niederreiter, Uniform Distribution of Sequences, Chapter I, Exercise 4.3, p. 40: “For real θ with |θ| > 1, the sequence (θ^n x) is u.d. mod 1 for almost all x.” See https://web.maths.unsw.edu.au/~josefdick/preprints/KuipersNied_book.pdf. Flatto, Lagarias and Pollington, “On the range of fractional parts {ξ(p/q)^n},” Acta Arithmetica 70 (1995), p. 128, states that for γ = 4/65, Z_{3/2}(γ,1−γ) has positive Hausdorff dimension and hence is uncountable, citing Pollington (1981). Its definition on p. 126 imposes the interval condition for every n ≥ 0. https://doi.org/10.4064/aa-70-2-125-147
findings.suggested_fix: To state the book’s multiplier result, replace the universal transcendence hypothesis with `∀ᵐ (x : ℝ) ∂MeasureTheory.volume, IsEquidistributedModuloOne (fun n ↦ x * (3 / 2 : ℝ) ^ n)`, cite Exercise 4.3, and categorize this replacement as textbook. If an open arithmetic variant was intended instead, obtain a source for that variant rather than asserting the claim for all transcendental multipliers.

reformulations.difference: The supporting definition counts indices 0,…,N−1 and uses closed test intervals, including singleton intervals. The book initially counts indices 1,…,N and uses half-open intervals.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: Changing the initial indexing changes each normalized count by at most 1/N. Uniform distribution gives frequency zero to each singleton, by enclosing it in intervals of arbitrarily small length; consequently closed and half-open interval counts have the same limits, and singleton tests add no condition. The book explicitly gives the closed-interval characterization and finite-term invariance in Exercises 1.4 and 1.7–1.8. The n=0 division convention therefore has no effect on this limit statement.

reformulations.difference: The file describes accumulation points using `x ∈ closure (Set.range s \ {x})`, rather than using subsequential limits or `MapClusterPt x atTop s`. The same representation is used in the other two accumulation-point problems.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: For s(n) = fract((3/2)^n), the fractional parts are pairwise distinct: their reduced rational denominators are 2^n. For an injective real sequence, accumulation of its range after removing x is equivalent to being a subsequential limit. Every punctured neighborhood then contains infinitely many relevant indices, and conversely a convergent subsequence cannot remain at x. The scratch file proves injectivity, the pointwise equivalence, and the equivalence of the two infinite-set statements. Although these notions differ for constant sequences, that distinction does not affect the power-sequence declarations; the generic forward implication in the helper theorem is also valid.

sources_consulted: L. Kuipers and H. Niederreiter, Uniform Distribution of Sequences (1974), especially Chapter I, Definition 1.1, Exercises 1.4 and 1.7–1.8, §4 including its notes and exercises, and Exercise 5.12: https://web.maths.unsw.edu.au/~josefdick/preprints/KuipersNied_book.pdf

L. Flatto, J. C. Lagarias and A. D. Pollington, On the range of fractional parts {ξ(p/q)^n}, Acta Arithmetica 70 (1995), especially pp. 125–128: https://doi.org/10.4064/aa-70-2-125-147 ; full text https://www.impan.pl/shop/publication/transaction/download/product/108521?download.pdf
K. Mahler, An unsolved problem on the powers of 3/2 (1968), introduction: https://doi.org/10.1017/S1446788700005371
Google Books edition and preview metadata: https://books.google.com/books?vid=ISBN9780486149998 and https://books.google.com/books?vid=ISBN9780486450193
https://mathoverflow.net/questions/150996/small-fractional-part-of-powers-of-a-real-number (question and comments, read through the Stack Exchange API)
https://mathoverflow.net/questions/62854/the-complexity-of-the-leading-fractional-bit-of-a-power-of-a-rational-number (question, answer and comments, read through the Stack Exchange API)
could_not_verify: Equidistribution.isAccumulationPoint_three_halves_pow: its predicate and real-valued answer slot were verified, but the cited book passage and Wikipedia page do not explicitly pose the task of finding one specific accumulation point. I could not independently confirm that added variant’s precise bibliographic source or its current open status.
review.notes: All seven declarations were inspected. `/workspace/review/scratch.lean` compiles without errors or warnings. Independent, sorry-free checks prove the helper subsequence theorem, the existential accumulation-point test, the accumulation-point equivalences, and the deduction refuting the transcendental claim from an uncountable exceptional set. Pollington’s uncountability result itself was checked in the literature, not formalized. Small fractional parts were evaluated, and the real answer slot was checked to be genuinely constrained (2 cannot be an answer). The solved infinite-limit-points tag agrees with the result attributed to Vijayaraghavan (1940). No files in the checkout were edited.

not_demonstrated.reason: An unconditional disproof requires establishing the existence of a transcendental multiplier whose fractional parts are not equidistributed. The reported argument obtains this from Pollington’s uncountable exceptional-set theorem, which is not available in the checked libraries and would require substantial formalization. The previous scratch lemma assumes such an uncountable set, so it does not itself refute the declaration as stated.

submission.summary: No short, honest unconditional proof or disproof was found. No trivial-proof file was created; the earlier conditional calculation is not being submitted as a demonstration.
submission.gave_up_reason: The only reported misformalization needs a nontrivial exceptional-set existence theorem to produce a counterexample. Proving that theorem is beyond a handful-line demonstration, and assuming it or using a sorry-backed declaration would not satisfy the requested rules.

submission.summary: Replaced the universal transcendental-multiplier claim with Lebesgue-almost-everywhere quantification over real multipliers, as in Chapter 1, Exercise 4.3. Renamed the theorem to Equidistribution.isEquidistributedModuloOne_ae_three_halves_pow, updated its docstring and source reference, and changed its category to textbook. Only the reported declaration was changed. The required compilation succeeds with only expected `declaration uses 'sorry'` warnings.
